claims.text: A predictive approach leveraging chemical disorder will identify low-phonon-thermal-conductivity HEAs more accurately than current heuristic or statistical models.
Explicit incorporation of configurational entropy and atomistic scattering mechanisms is the reason for the expected improvement in prediction accuracy.
The target materials are as-synthesized, single-phase HEAs having randomly distributed multielement solid-solution structures.
The proposed model integrates local atomic environments, mass mismatch, size mismatch, and entropy-derived parameters in a multiscale simulation framework.
Mass-disorder phonon scattering dominates from ambient to moderately elevated temperatures in the intended HEAs.
A random distribution of multiple elements enhances phonon scattering through mass disorder.
A random distribution of multiple elements enhances phonon scattering through bonding disorder.
Increased configurational disorder produces enhanced phonon scattering.
Enhanced phonon scattering caused by configurational disorder lowers phonon thermal conductivity.
Quantitatively linking local bonding environments and mass mismatch to phonon transport will provide more precise estimates of thermal-conductivity reduction.
Under optimal conditions, the proposed model will reduce prediction error by approximately 10–20% relative to existing methods.
Current prediction methods largely rely on empirical correlations or average properties without detailed atomistic resolution.
The lack of detailed atomistic resolution in current methods leads to larger discrepancies between predicted and measured thermal conductivity.
The expected improvement applies to single-phase, chemically disordered HEAs.
The approach may not apply to multiphase alloys.
The approach may not apply when electronic thermal conductivity dominates total thermal conductivity.
Experimental data specifically resolving phonon thermal conductivity in HEAs are limited.
Variability in alloy processing may alter the magnitude of the model's improvement.
TDTR can supply the phonon thermal-conductivity measurements required for the benchmark.
Failure to achieve an approximately 10–20% error reduction relative to the baseline, or failure to reproduce the predicted disorder-dependent trend, will falsify the hypothesis.
